title: How a false memory was planted

lines.text: Psychologists convinced adults they had been lost in a shopping mall as kids. It never happened.
In 1995, Elizabeth Loftus and Jacqueline Pickrell gave 24 people a booklet of four childhood stories.
Three were real, collected from their relatives.
One was fake: getting lost in a mall and rescued by an elderly stranger.
Over several days, people wrote down what they remembered.
About a quarter of them came to remember the fake event.
Their false memories were usually hazier than the real ones, but they felt real to them.
Critics argue it's harder to plant less believable events. But the point stands.
Memory isn't a recording. It's rebuilt every time you remember.
So how sure are you about your earliest memory?

sources.claim: Loftus and Pickrell (1995): 24 participants, four childhood narratives (one false: lost in a mall); about 25% remembered the false event; critics note plausibility matters

publish.title: Scientists Planted a Fake Childhood Memory 🧠
publish.description: The 1995 'lost in the mall' study showed how easily memories can be rebuilt. A quarter of people remembered something that never happened.
publish.pinned_comment: Do you have a memory you're not sure really happened? 👇
